An Israeli army soldier looks at destroyed buildings in the Gaza Strip as troops stand on the boundary with the Palestinian territory, on 13 August 2025 (Jack Guez/AFP)

Israeli military suicides reach 16-year high
A total of 23 serving Israeli military personnel have died by suicide since the beginning of this year, the highest number recorded in the army since 2010, Haaretz reported on Monday.
At least 17 former soldiers also died by suicide in the past year, shortly after being discharged from military service, bringing the total number of serving and former soldiers who took their own lives to 40.
Suicides are not confined to Israel's military. Haaretz noted that five police officers also died by suicide in 2026.
According to official Israeli military data cited by the report, 73 officers and soldiers have died by suicide since the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on 7 October.
However, the actual number of war-related suicides is likely to be much higher, as the military's figures include only personnel who died while still serving.
"This war is an unprecedented event in terms of the level of distress and burnout of the soldiers who took part in it," a mental health academic at the University of Haifa told Haaretz.
"The coming years are critical, perhaps even dramatic, with regard to suicide rates."
Israeli officer warns of ‘Jewish terrorism’
An Israeli senior military officer has warned that attacks by settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are organised and involve thousands of people, Israel's Channel 12 News reported on Monday.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Exclusive: Guatemala circulates proposal to curb ICC powers in line with US-Israeli demands
data.author: Sondos Asem
data.summary:
Exclusive: Guatemala circulates proposal to curb ICC powers in line with US-Israeli demands
Submitted by
Sondos Asem
on
Sat, 11/21/2026 - 18:15
The Latin American country pitched the idea to diplomats in The Hague despite rights advocates warning against attempts to curb the court's mission
Donald Trump speaks as Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio listen during a news briefing in the White House on 20 November 2026 (AFP)
Off
Guatemala has circulated a proposal to member states of the International Criminal Court (ICC) that closely echoed demands made by the United States and Israel to severely restrict the court's powers, Middle East Eye can reveal.
The three-page paper was submitted at a closed-door retreat for ambassadors from ICC member states in The Hague on 18 November, less than two weeks before the court's Assembly of States Parties (ASP) opens its annual session.
The proposal advocated for dialogue with the US over curbing the ICC's ability to pursue cases involving nationals of countries that aren't members of the court, such as the US, Israel and Russia.
MEE understands that Washington's G7 allies, including the UK, Germany and Italy, expressed a readiness to discuss similar proposals with the US but were reluctant to advocate the idea publicly.
As a result, Guatemala, a Latin American country allied with Israel and the US, decided to take the lead and draft the proposal.
The document, seen by MEE, reflects Washington's longstanding opposition to the prosecution of Israeli leaders and the court's ability to also prosecute US officials for crimes committed on the territory of member states.
The paper floats requiring consent from a suspect's country of nationality even when the alleged crimes took place on the territory of an ICC member state.

data.title: Middle East Eye: India's Rafale fighter jet count reduced by three after 2025 aerial battles with Pakistan
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
India's Rafale fighter jet count reduced by three after 2025 aerial battles with Pakistan
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 13:01
Listing by World Air Forces increases scrutiny of India's denial of losses in conflict with Pakistan in 2025
A pilot climbs into a Rafale fighter jet before a French-Indian military exercise at Mont-de-Marsan air base, southwestern France, 26 November 2025 (Christophe Archambault/AFP).
Off
The number of active Rafale fighter jets in the Indian Air Force has fallen to 32 from 35 in the latest edition of an international military aviation directory, which has stirred renewed scrutiny of India's May 2025 military confrontation with Pakistan.
The revised figures, which appear in the 2027 World Air Forces directory published by British aviation magazine FlightGlobal, have renewed questions about the extent of Indian losses during Operation Sindoor.
Following the 22 April 2025 Pahalgam attack in Indian-administered Kashmir, India launched the military campaign on 7 May and attacked several targets deep inside Pakistan.
In the largest jet engagements of the 21st century, over 114 fighter jets were mobilised and engaged across the border.
Some 72 Indian Air Force (IAF) aircraft and 42 Pakistan Air Force (PAF) aircraft engaged each other in a confrontation that lasted roughly 50 minutes, according to military briefings and defence analyses.
Pakistan claimed to have shot down six Indian military aircraft, including three Rafales, during the confrontation.
New Delhi disputed the scale of Islamabad's claims but did not publish a detailed account of its own aircraft losses.
During a military briefing on 11 May, Air Marshal Awadhesh Kumar Bharti acknowledged that India had suffered aircraft losses but declined to identify the number or types involved.
“We are in a combat scenario and losses are a part of combat,” Bharti said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel likely to lose Gaza genocide case if ICJ follows Myanmar ruling, Tel Aviv scholar says
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Israel likely to lose Gaza genocide case if ICJ follows Myanmar ruling, Tel Aviv scholar says
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 14:00
Israeli law professor Eliav Lieblich says language used by Myanmar officials mild compared to Netanyahu, Ben Gvir and others
Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu looks on during a speech at the Israeli Knesset during the opening day of the new parliament in Jerusalem on 10 November 2026 (AFP)
Off
Israel will probably lose the genocide case brought by South Africa if the International Court of Justice (ICJ) applies the reasoning it used last week to find Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, an Israeli international law scholar has said.
“It is very bad that we have reached this point. It is a real earthquake,” said Eliav Lieblich, a professor at Tel Aviv University’s law faculty.
“Before jumping to conspiracy theories about the court, Israel has mainly itself to blame,” he wrote in a series of posts in Hebrew on X. “Even if you disagree with the majority on every legal point, no reasonable country should come anywhere close to falling short of the standards it set. In many respects, Netanyahu’s government dug this hole itself.”
The ICJ on Thursday concluded in a 9-6 decision that Myanmar's security forces had committed genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2017 operations.
The judgment, the first time the UN's highest court has found a state responsible for genocide, offers South Africa a significant legal precedent in its case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, particularly over how judges assess genocidal intent when a state claims its military actions are driven by security objectives.
To prove the genocide, the ICJ first had to prove that genocidal acts were committed, then that there was a “specific intent” by the Myanmar state to destroy the group.

Miss Israel was booed on stage during the national costume portion of the Miss Universe pageant in Puerto Rico this weekend.
As Danielle Yablonka stepped out in a gold jewelled bodice, boots and crown, she spread her arms to reveal a cape depicting olive trees and Jaffa oranges, with the word “peace” written in English, Hebrew and Arabic running along the bottom.
After she came to a stop and posed for the judges, she was immediately met with loud boos that even the music couldn’t cover.
Turning around to reveal the back of the garment, she kept her arms held out to show the audience the warm-toned depiction of East Jerusalem, featuring the vibrant gold and blue of Al-Aqsa Mosque complex in the centre, surrounded by the Old City.
East Jerusalem is considered occupied under international law. It is also envisioned as the capital of an independent Palestinian state - not a part of Israel.
The glossy image - not a real photo - did not reflect the ongoing demolition of Palestinian homes in the city, and featured the word Jerusalem in English, Hebrew and Arabic.
The costume choice for the 25-year-old Miami-born model was met with fierce criticism on social media, with users pointing out the ongoing ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and the genocide in Gaza.

The US is weighing a plan to train Syrian soldiers in demining in what would be the first US military training mission in Syria since President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power.
Reuters reported on Monday that the training operation is still under discussion, but if it is agreed it will mark a return of US troops to Syria after they have just completed a withdrawal.
The last remaining US troops left their last base in Hasakah, Syria, in April, ending a 10-year presence in the country.
The US kept thousands of soldiers in Syria as part of operations to defeat the Islamic State (IS) group. At least 2,000 US troops remained in the country ostensibly to defeat IS but also to counter Iran.
In 2024, Ahmed al-Sharaa led a military offensive that ousted Bashar al-Assad, an Iranian ally, from power.
The programme would be part of the Damascus Coordination Center, set up last year in Jordan to facilitate cooperation between Syrian authorities, the US and its regional allies. Reuters said that cooperation could be expanded beyond demining.
The return of US troops would come at a time when Saudi Arabia, a key US ally, is looking to Syrian military advisers to help fight the Houthis in Yemen. A western official previously told MEE that some Syrian drone specialists had already arrived in Yemen to assist the Saudi-backed forces.

data.author: Omar Ashour

The strategic test is whether repeated attacks constrain Moscow’s ability to sustain its war and overseas military deployments
A satellite image shows smoke rising from a burning ship in the Libyan port of Benghazi. Ukraine claimed it was behind strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on 23 November, 2026 (AFP)
Off
On Monday, hours after Ukraine claimed responsibility for the drone attack that sank Russian warship at Libyan naval base, Ukraine Security Service (SBU) said in a statement that "Russia’s military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes even far beyond the Black Sea."
The wreckage at Benghazi gave that warning substance.
Kyiv says seven Ukrainian naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury, destroyed its Ka-27 helicopter and also struck the weapons transport ship MV Angara.
Satellite imagery showed the corvette capsized. Commissioned in 2023, Merkury was a modern combatant, designed to fight ships and submarines and defend against air attack. Ukraine - a country deprived of most of its conventional navy as of 2014 following Russia's annexation of Crimea - is extending maritime attrition into Russia’s Mediterranean foothold in 2026.
As previously argued in Middle East Eye, maritime denial can defeat a superior navy’s strategic objectives without winning conventional fleet battles.
Benghazi is the latest proof.
A campaign across seas
The 11 named vessels in Ukrainian-claimed or suspected incidents since August 2025 illustrate four overlapping target sets. The first is "sea combatants", exemplified by Merkury.
The second is "military transport": Angara was struck near Benghazi while Sparta II was hit in the Gulf of Finland while bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Jared Kushner says Israel becoming 'global-pariah state'
In an interview with New York Magazine, US special envoy Jared Kushner said Israel is on a path toward becoming a "global-pariah state."
Kushner, who has been highly active in Middle East negotiations, described Israel as standing at a crossroads after October 7.
"[Israel] could be much more secure and integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward a global-pariah state," Kushner said.
